title: Council receives 2025 budget with 3.9% tax increase
subtitle: Conflict declarations, off-street parking by-laws, and investments in recreation, housing and the strategic plan
overview: Council met in a special session to deal with the Mayor's proposed 2025 budget. Under provincial legislation the budget is a mayor's budget. No amendments were submitted by the deadline, so it was considered adopted. Council then formally received it and directed staff to implement it {{vote:m1}}.

The budget includes a 3.9% tax rate increase, which the minutes put at about $49 a year for the average home. The mayor said the city has kept existing service levels while responding to growth. The mayor also said average increases over ten years have stayed below Ontario inflation. Highlighted investments include a new southwest library branch, the Rosenberg Community Centre, the Kitchener Indoor Recreation Facility at Schlegel Park, parks and tree canopy work, and affordable housing funding.

Three councillors declared conflicts on parts of the budget. Those parts were voted on separately, and the rest was approved on a recorded vote. Council also gave third reading to by-laws amending off-street parking regulations, and these did not relate to the budget. The meeting lasted about 40 minutes.

decisions.detail: Council received the Mayor's proposed 2025 budget, which includes a 3.9% tax rate increase, and directed staff to implement it {{vote:m1}}.
Council gave third reading to three by-laws amending By-law 88-169 on municipal off-street parking facilities (Schedules A, B and C).

debate: Councillors said staff do most of the heavy lifting on the budget, and they praised staff and the finance team for balancing services with affordability.
One councillor said it is easy to spend beyond your means or to keep taxes low by cutting services. They said the city has avoided both.

Another councillor said residents often ask for tax cuts, but the real choice is between cutting services such as snow clearing and recreation programs or maintaining them with a responsible levy increase.

Several councillors compared the smooth process with other councils and the regional budget debate. They said a shared vision has made budgets easier than in earlier years, when line-by-line debates ran long.
The mayor pointed to growth pressures and the need to maintain about $10 billion in city assets. The mayor also noted over $200 million in federal and provincial funding secured over five years.
